newsitem.title: USA: Fund information on the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Fund information on the Internet.

text.p: These days, anyone can get on the Internet. Even if you don't have a computer and a modem, your office probably does. Better yet, you can trot down to the local library or coffee shop and make a connection.
Naturally, a computer can't plan your mutual fund investments for you. But with more than 8,000 funds to choose from, it's a good idea to get as much information about funds as you can.

A few years ago, that meant lots of trips to the library or the broker's office -- or else buying expensive subscriptions to investment newsletters. Now, you can get the information you need instantly, with the click of a computer key. That information can help you make decisions about how to invest.

Dozens of independent fund websites provide detailed mutual fund performance data, as well as analyses of different funds and advice about investment strategies. In addition, many mutual fund companies have their own websites, which provide information about their funds.

If you're interested in tapping into those resources, the best advice is to surf the web for an afternoon to check out your options. Then you can decide which sites are most useful for different purposes -- choosing funds, finding out more about a fund you own, or creating a portfolio strategy that works for you.

Some sites require you to pay for services or information. For example, at InvesTools (http://www.investools.com), which provides research on stocks and funds, you pay $5 apiece for Morningstar fund reports. But most sites also provide a variety of useful services at no charge.

NetWorth (http://networth.quicken.com/investments) is one place to cruise for ideas and information. The site allows you to sort through more than 7,000 funds to find the ones that suit your criteria -- which can include factors such as past performance, sales charges, investment minimums and the like. It also provides detailed information about individual funds once you have narrowed your list of candidates. The site also offers book reviews, articles and other information about investing, as well as portfolio tracking tools and fund-picking tools.

Mutual Funds Interactive (http://www.brill.com) doesn't include fund screening tools. It does, however, provide free information about funds, including fund basics, profiles of fund managers and interviews with fund experts.

The Mutual Fund Investor's Center (http://www.mfea.com) allows investors to "visit" 42 fund companies for information about their offerings. You can use the site to order information from fund sponsors, screen for appropriate fund choices, read educational materials and develop an investment plan for meeting goals, such as retirement or college for children.

Invest-O-Rama (http://www.investorama.com) is a fun and easy way to quickly navigate to more than 4,300 investment related sites, including over 100 fund family home pages. The site also features a wide range of resources that can help individuals learn more about personal finance and investing -- such as a stock selection guide tutorial and articles with how-to advice and market commentary.
Unlike third-party websites, fund company home pages aren't going to give you information that will steer you to their competition. But they can provide useful services.

For example, T. Rowe Price (http://www.troweprice.com) offers daily updates of T. Rowe Price funds' performance and weekly summaries of the financial markets. It also provides a wealth of investor education materials, including articles and an investment strategy planner that can help you create an asset allocation strategy.

Fidelity's On-Line Investor Center (http://www.fid-inv.com) also provides educational services and planning tools for investors. For example: If you choose Investment & Retirement Planning, you can calculate how much you need to save for retirement, based on information you provide about your salary, age and so on. That could even save you an expensive trip to a financial planner.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
